title: Wet method versus dry method for caramel
subtitle: When to dissolve sugar in water first, and when to melt it straight in the pan
excerpt: Caramel can be made by melting sugar directly in a dry pan (the dry method) or by dissolving it in water first before reducing it to caramel (the wet method). The wet method is more forgiving and easier to control. The dry method is faster. Both produce caramel from the same sugar at the same temperature.
sourceNotes: Wet and dry caramel methods are standard teaching points in confectionery and patisserie. The technical difference is well-established: the water in the wet method simply provides a medium for even heating before boiling off.

recipe.freezeNotes: Caramel sauce freezes well in a sealed jar for up to 3 months. Reheat gently.
recipe.batchNotes: Use a wider, heavier pan for larger batches so the sugar heats evenly.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Caramel sauce keeps in the fridge for 2 weeks in a sealed jar.

glossaryTerms.definition: The reforming of sugar into solid crystals during or after heating, which turns caramel gritty and opaque. The wet method reduces the risk of crystallisation; avoiding stirring once the syrup boils also prevents it.

content.text: Both methods produce the same caramel. The difference is how you handle the sugar during cooking. The wet method is easier for beginners: the water keeps the sugar fluid while it dissolves, giving more time before the temperature reaches the point where burning can happen.

Put 200 g caster sugar in a wide, heavy saucepan with 60 ml cold water. Set over medium heat and stir gently until the sugar dissolves completely, before the syrup begins to boil. Once boiling, stop stirring. Clip on the thermometer and cook without touching the pan until the syrup reaches the colour you want (175°C for a medium-deep amber). If crystals form on the sides of the pan, brush them back in with a damp pastry brush.

Put the sugar directly into the dry pan over medium heat. Do not stir. As the edges begin to melt, use a heatproof spatula to push the dry sugar toward the liquid. The sugar melts unevenly; swirl the pan gently to even it out. The dry method produces caramel faster but is harder to control: the outer edges can burn while the centre is still dry. Wet method: caramel sauce, caramel tarts, creme caramel, any recipe where you pour the caramel into a mould or mix it with cream. More reliable for beginners and for large batches.

Dry method: praline, where a slightly more complex flavour from hot spots can add character. Also for small batches of caramel where the wetness of the wet method would require a long boil before the water evaporates.
Caramel at 175°C causes severe burns. If it touches skin, run cold water over it for at least ten minutes and seek medical care if needed.
